Epilogue: One Glad Morning
§ 19.1 — The Question of Error

To conclude a work built entirely on the discipline of methodological atheism requires us to confront the final, most difficult engineering check: What if I am wrong? This is not a casual intellectual puzzle, nor is it a rhetorical safety valve designed to appease religious critics at the last minute. For a book that treats Christianity as the objective description of the laws of human coordination, the possibility of structural error must be analyzed with the same rigor we apply to the joints of a timber f
rame or the load tolerances of a concrete bridge. We must run a plumb line over our own methodology and ask what occurs if the closed mechanical system we have mapped is actually open.

In the tradesman’s world, the check for error is the absolute prerequisite for stability. A carpenter does not double-check his framing square because he is anxious or because he doubts his own capacity; he checks it because he respects the reality of gravity. If the square is off by even a sixteenth of an inch at the corner, that error will compound across the span of the rafters until the ridge board drifts feet away from its target coordinate, and the roof splits under the first heavy winter snow. The mi

stake is not a moral failing; it is a physical deviation that accumulates in the timeline. Likewise, in compiling this method, I must ask if my baseline assumption—that the universe is a closed circuit of cause and effect—contains a compounding error that has thrown my entire reading of history out of square.

Let us trace this accumulation of error through the practice of land surveying. Consider a surveyor attempting to lay out the boundary lines of a major subdivision across the broken, timbered terrain of the Orange County hills. The surveyor uses a transit, a high-precision telescope mounted on a tripod, to sight the reference monuments and project straight lines through the brush. If the transit’s optical axis is out of calibration by a tiny fraction of a degree—an error so small it cannot be detected by th

e naked eye—the first fifty feet of the boundary line will appear perfectly aligned with the monument. The surveyor will walk through the briars, clearing the line of sight, driving cedar stakes into the red clay, confident in his measurements. But as the line is projected further across the hills, the deviation compounds. By the time the surveyor reaches the far corner of the valley, a mile away from the starting point, the boundary line has drifted fifty feet to the left, cutting through the center of a n

eighbor’s barn and placing a public road in the middle of a swamp. The error was silent, invisible at the point of origin, but it registered itself in the geometry of the land. Sincerity does not correct the line. The surveyor may have worked with the greatest care, sweat, and diligence, but the boundary remains crooked, and the property records will remain in conflict until the transit is recalibrated and the work is redone from the baseline.

The same rule governs the pouring of a concrete foundation. Before the mixers arrive, the crew must build the wooden forms that will contain the wet stone. They measure the perimeter—thirty feet by fifty feet—and they verify that the opposite sides are equal. But if they do not check the diagonals, if they do not run a tape from corner to corner to verify that the cross-measurements are identical, they may pour a trapezoid rather than a rectangle. Once the concrete is poured, reinforced with steel rebar, an

d cured, the mistake is locked into the physical plane. The framers who arrive next cannot fix it. They can try to cheat the bottom plates over the edge of the concrete, tapering the sill to hide the twist, but the building remembers the error in its bones. As the walls rise, the corners will refuse to meet at ninety degrees. The roof rafters will be cut to different lengths to reach the ridge, the shingles will run crooked across the deck, and when the sheetrock is hung, the joints will crack under the set

tling weight of the rafters. Years later, the homeowner will find that the bedroom doors swing open on their own, the double-hung windows bind in their tracks during the damp spring months, and the foundation itself will crack under the uneven shear stress. The house is in constant tension, fighting the original twist that was poured into the concrete on day one.

Most modern debates about religious belief are structured around Pascal’s Wager—a dry, financial hedge that treats faith as an insurance policy. The wager asserts that if you believe in God and are wrong, you lose nothing, but if you do not believe and are wrong, you face eternal damnation. The tradesman rejects this logic immediately. You do not build a roof by hoping a structural failure won’t happen and buying a policy to cover the collapse; you build the roof to withstand the load. If the structure is o

ut of plumb, no amount of insurance will keep the beam from cracking when the weight sits heavy on it. The wager treats God as a gullible landlord who can be fooled by a lease agreement signed in bad faith, and it treats belief as a verbal token rather than a physical alignment of choices. It suggests that a verbal profession of faith can insulate a man from the mechanical consequences of a disordered life. Our question is different. We are not asking how to hedge our bets; we are asking how the coordinate
system of our lives behaves under the load of absolute error.

If the methodology of this book is correct—if the universe is a closed mechanical system and Christianity is the historical discovery of the objective laws of human social preservation—then the alignment of choice with the covenant is the only way to resist entropic decay. In this scenario, the methodological atheist who cancels debt, lives blamelessly, and protects the substrate is simply aligning his 4D worldline with the physical laws of human survival. He does not need to believe in the Giver to benefit

from the gift, just as an aerodynamicist does not need to worship the wind to build a wing that generates lift. The wing works because of its curvature, not because of the pilot’s theology. The lift is a physical consequence of the air flowing over the geometry of the wing, and that lift holds the weight of the aircraft regardless of what the crew believes about the origin of the atmosphere.

But what if I am wrong? What if the universe is not a closed mechanical circuit? What if the historical memory of Christ is not merely the trace of human coordination stabilizing under pressure, but the literal, physical intervention of the Creator of the timeline? If I am wrong in this direction, then the materialist method is not a description of the ultimate reality; it is merely a description of the floor plan. It means I have spent years tracing the load paths of the house, analyzing the thickness of t

he walls, and measuring the square of the joints, while remaining completely blind to the Architect who designed the house and still resides in it. This epilogue is the analysis of that error, and of what it would cost to correct it.
§ 19.2 — The Scaffolding of Belief
If we are to answer what it would take for me to become a “true believer,”

we must first define what belief actually is within the cognitive framework of this book. The modern church and the secular critic both treat belief as a simple act of the will—a decision to accept a set of metaphysical propositions as true, like choosing to believe that it will rain tomorrow. But under the Lens-Human-Construct (L-H-C) model, this definition is structurally impossible. The human mind is not a free-floating spirit that can choose its own inputs; it is a physical sensor situated within a cont
inuous timeline, constrained by the feedback loops of its environment.

To believe in the literal, supernatural claims of theology—to believe that a man walked on water, that water turned to wine, and that a dead body was physically reanimated in violation of the second law of thermodynamics—requires a coordinate system that is not present in my physical environment. The mind is a pattern-recognition engine. It builds its expectations based on the consistency of the physical plane: gravity pulls downward, electricity flows along the path of least resistance, and wood decays whe

n exposed to moisture. These are not opinions; they are invariants. To force the mind to accept a metaphysical claim that directly contradicts these invariants would require breaking the very tools of observation and verification that keep us sane. It would require the intentional introduction of cognitive drift, allowing the mind to steer by imaginary coordinates that do not correspond to the physical feedback of the timeline.

Let us illustrate this with the calibration of machine tools. Suppose you are turning a steel axle on a manual metal lathe, aiming to fit a sleeve bearing with a tolerance of five ten-thousandths of an inch. To measure your progress, you mount a dial indicator against the carriage. The dial is a delicate instrument; a spring-loaded plunger translates the physical displacement of the metal into the rotation of a needle over a calibrated face. If a microscopic speck of metal dust, floating off the cutting too

l, slips past the felt seal and lodges between the gears behind the dial face, the needle will stick. The operator turns the handwheel, reading the dial, believing he is cutting the steel to the exact coordinate. But when he slides the micrometer over the finished axle, he discovers the steel is three thousandths of an inch too small, and the part is ruined. The operator cannot solve this by having
“faith”

in the dial indicator. He cannot look at the stuck needle and wish it to be correct, nor can he declare his loyalty to the manufacturer of the tool. The tool is out of registration. Sincerity will not make the sleeve bearing fit the axle. The operator must stop the lathe, dismantle the indicator, clean the gears with solvent, blow them out with dry air, and verify the needle’s movement against a set of hardened steel gauge blocks of known dimensions. The dial is not an object of belief; it is an instrument
of verification, and it must be calibrated to the invariant standard of the physical plane.
To bypass these safety subroutines of the brain—to train oneself to accept metaphysical assertions as physical facts without confirmation—is like gluing the needle of a pressure gauge to the “safe”

green zone. It makes the engine room crew feel comfortable, and it allows them to work without fear, but it does not stop the boiler plates from tearing apart when the steam pressure exceeds the tensile strength of the steel plates. The safety subroutines of the human brain are not design flaws; they are the cognitive levels and plumb lines that prevent us from walking off cliffs or eating rotten food. If you systematically override these sensors to fit into a social group or to escape the terror of mortali

ty, you introduce a permanent offset into your coordinate system. You lose the ability to tell what is level, and that drift will eventually bleed into the choices you make regarding the material welfare of your family and your neighbors.

Consider the phenomenon of hydrogen embrittlement in structural steel. If you expose a high-strength steel bolt to atomic hydrogen—either during the acid-pickling process or through environmental corrosion—the tiny hydrogen atoms, being the smallest elements in the universe, will diffuse into the crystal lattice of the metal. They lodge themselves in the interstitial voids between the iron atoms. From the outside, the bolt appears completely healthy. The threads are clean, the zinc coating is bright, and it

can be tightened down to its specified torque without showing any signs of weakness. But at the microscopic level, the trapped hydrogen atoms prevent the iron crystals from sliding and locking under stress. The steel loses its ductility and becomes brittle. The moment a heavy tensile load is applied, the bolt snaps clean in two with a sound like a pistol shot, without stretching or yielding first. This is the structural consequence of Gnostic self-deception. When a man fills his cognitive framework with un

verified assertions and magical coordinates to avoid the hard work of material observation, he introduces hydrogen embrittlement into his reason. Under the sudden load of personal tragedy, grief, or economic collapse, he shatters because there is no ductile material left in his mind to absorb the stress.

The barrier to belief is therefore not pride, nor is it the stubborn vanity of the intellectual who refuses to bow before a higher power. It is a commitment to the reality of the timeline. I cannot believe in the supernatural because my mind is calibrated to the plumb line of physical consequence. If I were to pretend to believe—to stand in the pew and declare that I accept the metaphysical dogmas of literalist theology—I would be introducing a lie into the center of my coordination circuit. I would be like

a carpenter who knows a wall is out of plumb but tells his helper it is straight to avoid the labor of rebuilding it. The lie would corrupt the work, leading to systemic drift and eventual collapse under load. I must remain on the ground where the measurements can be verified, checking the level of the lumber with my own eyes and refusing to steer by stars I cannot see.
§ 19.3 — The Complex Underpinning

This simple answer—that it would take me being wrong—carries an extremely complex underpinning that relies on the entire methodology of this book. To understand why this is the only logical conclusion, we must trace the load paths of our entire analysis, from the collapse of animism to the emergence of the Co-Construct.

If the universe is a closed mechanical system, then animism is a primitive, provisional interface that must be outgrown. The mind projects intention onto the world because it cannot calculate the mechanics of its environment, but once the mechanical laws are discovered, the ghosts must be stripped from the machinery. Physics replaces superstition because physics works. Spacetime curvature, entropy, and the conservation of momentum are the invariants that govern all physical motion. When we apply this logic

to human behavior, morality ceases to be a list of metaphysical commands and becomes a description of social forces. Order requires work; decay happens automatically. The covenant is the layout plan that prevents human coordination from rotting under the entropic pull of individual greed and imperial extraction.

But if the system is open—if the Creator of the physical plane is real—then this entire mechanical analysis is not negated; it is merely recontextualized. Mechanism is not negation. Let us consider the example of the water cycle. Before the development of modern meteorology, men believed that rain was a direct, localized act of a sky deity opening windows in heaven to pour water onto the crops. When we discovered that solar radiation warms the oceans, evaporating water vapor into the atmosphere where it ris

es, cools, condenses into clouds, and precipitates under gravity, we did not destroy the rain. We did not make the water any less wet, nor did we make the crops grow any less because we understood the cycle. We simply mapped the path of its movement. The water cycle is the mechanical explanation, but it does not tell you why water has the specific heat capacity it has, why hydrogen and oxygen bond at a precise angle of 104.5 degrees to create a polar molecule that makes life possible, or why there is a time
line for the rain to fall upon. The mechanism is the layout plan; it is not the explanation of the origin of the materials.

If the Creator exists, then the laws of human coordination I have mapped are the literal house rules of His creation. The Sermon on the Mount is not an arbitrary list of spiritual suggestions; it is the physical geometry of the Kingdom, the layout plan designed by the Architect to ensure that His creatures can live together without destroying the house. When Christ says to turn the other cheek, to give your cloak also, to love your enemies, He is not providing a list of pious virtues that violate the laws o

f nature; He is describing the only geometry that can absorb the kinetic energy of violence without transmitting it back into the structure as destructive oscillation. If you strike back, you feed the resonance. It is like an engine with an unbalanced flywheel; the vibration builds until the main bearings seize and the connecting rods punch a hole through the cast-iron engine block. The covenant is the engineering manual for the human coordination engine.

This means that the materialist method is not the opposite of belief; it is its physical substrate. The true believer who has spiritualized his faith into a Gnostic escape is actually further from the covenant than the methodological atheist who works the vineyard. The Gnostic believer asserts the metaphysical truth of the container while ignoring the physical demands of the content. He argues about the Giver while violating the objective laws of the gift. But the materialist, by aligning his choices with t
he physical coordinates of coordination, is executing the plan even if he does not recognize the designer.

Consider a blind mason laying brick in a dark, subterranean tunnel. He cannot see the sky, he cannot see the blueprint, and he cannot see the face of the master builder who drew the plans. But he has a line level, a plumb bob, and a trowel. By feeling the tension of the cord with his calloused fingertips and checking the plumb line against the steady pull of gravity, he lays each course of brick level and straight. The wall rises, strong and square, capable of supporting the massive weight of the stone arch

above it. Meanwhile, at the mouth of the tunnel, a sighted supervisor stands under a lamp, holding the paper blueprint. The supervisor shouts to the workers, praises the genius of the architect, and debates the quality of the mortar mixes, but he never picks up a trowel or lifts a single brick. If the master builder returns to inspect the work, he will not put a level on the supervisor’s words or his knowledge of the blueprint. He will walk into the dark tunnel and place his straightedge against the wall.

The wall built by the blind mason stands because it is aligned with gravity; the supervisor’s empty space collapses. If I am wrong, the difference between the believer and myself is not a difference in direction; it is a difference in sight. The complex underpinning of my error would reveal that the mechanical laws of coordination are not self-existing truths, but covenanted boundaries established by the Architect, and that my methodological atheism was merely the lens through which I was forced to observe
their alignment.
§ 19.4 — The Parable of the Two Sons

This structural relationship between verbal token and physical action is explained in the scriptures through a simple, tradesman-like parable. In Matthew 21:28-31, Christ addresses the religious managers of His day with a question that upends their entire system of authority:

“But what think ye? A certain man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard. He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went. And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not. Whether of them twain did the will of his father? They say unto him, The first. Jesus saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.”

Let us analyze this parable through the materialist lens we have developed. The father does not ask his sons for a profession of loyalty, a theological declaration, or an emotional experience. He asks for physical labor: “go work to day in my vineyard.” The vineyard is the substrate—the field of social coordination where crops must be planted, watered, weeded, and harvested to sustain the life of the family and the community. It requires tools, sweat, and time.

Let us look closely at the physical environment of the vineyard. The vineyard is not a pristine park or an abstract ledger of assets. It is a hillside of heavy, iron-red clay that bakes like brick under the summer sun. It is choked with wild blackberry brambles, poison ivy, and sumac that must be cut back with a brush hook. The cedar posts that support the rusty wire trellises have rotted at the ground level, and they must be dug out with a post-hole digger and replaced with new timber. The vines themselves

require careful, labor-intensive pruning, cutting back the dead wood to allow the new shoots to receive the sap. It is dirty, exhausting work that leaves a man’s lower back aching from swinging a mattock, his hands sliced by the wire and thorn, and his boots caked with red mud.
The first son is the methodological atheist. When commanded to work, he answers plainly and rudely: “I will not.”

He rejects the father’s authority, denies the metaphysical obligation, and insists on his own independence. He refuses to say the words that would satisfy the father’s dignity. But afterward, he looks at the vineyard, sees the weeds overtaking the vines, realizes that if the fruit dies, the family will starve, repents of his passivity, and goes into the field. He picks up the shovel, clears the stones, and does the physical labor of coordination. His choice is aligned with the invariants of the vineyard, ev

en though his mouth denied the owner. He spends his day in the dirt, dealing with weeds, thorns, heat, and physical exhaustion. His boots are covered in mud, and his hands are calloused. He does not talk about the father; he simply does the work that keeps the father’s household alive. He carries the heavy stones to rebuild the terrace walls so the soil doesn’t wash away in the summer thunderstorms. He clears the trash that has accumulated in the drainage ditches.
Contrast this with the second son, who represents the Gnostic believer. When commanded to work, he answers with immediate, polished compliance: “I go, sir.” He uses the title “sir”

(kyrios) with perfect cadence, validating the father’s authority and making a public declaration of his obedience. But he does not go into the field. He stays in the shade of the porch, drinks sweet tea, and reads the deeds and boundary surveys of the estate. He flatters himself with his status as a son, and leaves the vineyard to rot under the weeds. His words are aligned with the father’s name, but his feet are stationary. He contributes zero kinetic energy to the vineyard. He stands in the shade, discuss

ing the blueprint of the farm and the nobility of the father’s character, while the crops rot in the field from neglect. He represents the Gnostic manager who lives on the administrative tribute extracted from the farm, mistake-ridden and blind to the physical reality of the work.

Christ’s conclusion is absolute: it is the first son who did the will of the father. The publicans and the harlots—the social outcasts, the secular workers, the ones who make no claim to holiness but perform the raw labor of survival—enter the kingdom before the religious managers who have enclosed the name of God but abandoned the work. The will of the Father is not a verbal token; it is a physical measurement in the timeline. If the methodology of this book has led me to stand with the first son—to say

“I do not believe” while working the vineyard of mutual aid, debt cancellation, and blameless labor—then I am content to let the timeline judge the work. The labor of the first son is the physical implementation of the covenant, and that labor is what remains in motion.
§ 19.5 — The Hidden Leaven and the Unaffiliated Worker
This hidden, silent operation of the covenant is described in another parable of scale. In Matthew 13:33, Christ declares:
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.”
Let us analyze this process with the eye of a breadmaker. Leaven—which we know as yeast,
Saccharomyces cerevisiae

—is a microscopic unicellular organism. When a woman takes a pinch of it and mixes it into three measures of meal (which is about fifty pounds of flour), the yeast completely disappears. It is hidden in the flour. You cannot see it, you cannot count it, and it makes no public declaration of its presence. It has no flag, no organizational charter, and no voice. But it is not inert. In the warm, dark moisture of the dough, the yeast goes to work at the biochemical level. It releases enzymes that break down th

e complex starches of the wheat into simple sugars. It consumes these sugars, metabolizing them and releasing carbon dioxide gas and ethanol as waste products. The carbon dioxide molecules, trapped within the wet gluten matrix of the flour, expand as they warm. They stretch the microscopic sheets of protein, creating a million tiny pockets of air. This stretches the gluten grid, transforming a dense, heavy, inedible mass of wet flour and water into a rising, aerated dough that can be baked into a light, nou

rishing loaf. The yeast does not build a separate, external structure; it works quietly within the substrate, transforming the material properties of the dough. It works in the dark, without visibility, yet it objectively changes the physical outcome of the bread.

This is how the materialist method functions. It does not require the visible, administrative containers of the institutional church. It does not need the slogans, the fog machines, or the marketing budgets of the corporate LLCs. It is hidden in the everyday labor of the working class, working quietly beneath the surface to lift the substrate of cooperation, transforming the bread of community from a dense, flat lump of survival into a rising, shared abundance.

Because this work is hidden and unaffiliated, it is often rejected by the managers of the religious enclosure. In Mark 9:38-40, we read of a confrontation between the disciples and an unaffiliated worker:

“And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part.”

The disciples are operating within the logic of the administrative container. They see a man performing real, observable work—casting out the demons of madness, isolation, and despair—but they forbid him because “he followeth not us.”

He does not carry their credentials, he does not attend their assemblies, and he does not submit to their management. They care more about brand loyalty and organizational alignment than the actual relief of human suffering. But Christ upends their enclosure. He commands them to leave the worker alone, establishing the invariant law: “he that is not against us is on our part.”

I am this unaffiliated worker. I do not follow the institutional assemblies, I do not repeat the metaphysical dogmas, and I do not carry the credentials of the church managers. But I spent my years speaking with people about Christ, and using the coordinates of His covenant to help them cast out the demons of loneliness, distraction, and the suffocating self-deception of modern life. I have pointed them to the plumb line of scripture to steady their minds, and I have stood in the dirt to help them carry the

weight of their physical load. The work is unaffiliated, but it is not against Him. By helping the broken align their trajectories, severing social debts through forgiveness, and restoring their capacity to labor, I am doing the work of the vineyard in His name, even if I cannot see His face.
And as Christ says in the very next verse, Mark 9:41:
“For whosoever shall give you a cup of water to drink in my name, because ye belong to Christ, verily I say unto you, he shall not lose his reward.”

The cup of water is the simplest unit of physical aid. It requires no complex theology, no confession of faith, and no administrative container. It is the direct transfer of moisture to a dry throat, an act of physical coordination that supports the biological substrate of life. Surely, I would give a cup of water to a Christian. I would give it not as an act of patronizing charity, but as a recognition of shared labor. The folk who carry the name of Christ, who keep the churches open in the forgotten towns
of the Piedmont, who keep the oil burning in the lamps of memory—these are the folk who have preserved the root that supports us all.

Consider the Wednesday night church dinners in the fellowship hall. Long before the congregation arrives, the older women of the church are in the kitchen. They have been there since three in the afternoon, boiling large pots of potatoes, roasting chickens, and slicing bread. They set the folding tables, lay out the plastic forks, and mix the sweet tea. They do not know the history of the ecumenical councils, and they cannot debate the Greek morphology of the epistles. But they know that the young family do

wn the road is struggling to buy groceries, that the single mother needs a break, and that the elderly widower has not spoken to anyone all week. They serve the food, wash the heavy pots by hand, sweep the floors, and carry the trash bags out to the dumpster in the dark. This is not administrative management; it is the physical labor of coordination, the preservation of the cooperative substrate. Even when their theology is literalist and their institutions are captured by capital, their hands still carry t

he muscle memory of the covenant. They are the ones who teach their children to be good, who watch over the sick, and who refuse to let the memory of the Resurrection die in a culture that worships only the immediate profit of the extraction loops. Thank you for being Christians. Thank you for keeping the root alive while the rest of the world was trying to pave it over. Your faith has maintained the soil in which this method could grow, and for that, the tradesman owes you a debt of gratitude that no intel
lectual critique can erase.
§ 19.6 — One Glad Morning

This brings us to the final coordinate of the worldline. If the methodology of this book is correct, then when my physical trajectory terminates, my 4D time snake will simply end. The kinetic energy of my life will dissipate into the substrate, the memories will fade, and the work I have contributed to the coordination of my community will remain in motion as the only trace of my existence. That is the limit of my sight, and it is a plumb line I have accepted without fear.
But what if I am wrong?

What if the old Protestant hymns of my childhood were not merely poetic expressions of human hope, but maps of an actual future? What if the timeline does not end in stasis, but opens up into that glad morning when this life is over? If I am wrong, and the grave is not the boundary but the gateway to the presence of the Giver, then my methodological atheism will collapse in a single moment of physical verification. The scaffolding will be stripped away, the lens will be made obsolete by direct sight, and I
will find myself standing before the cornerstone of the world.

If that glad morning arrives, I will not run. I will not hide in the ruins of my academic critiques, nor will I offer a complicated, dialectical defense of my skepticism. I will turn my eyes upon Jesus, look full in His wonderful face, and I will say three things.
First, I will say: “I was wrong.”

In a universe where error correction is the engine of development and the only path to sanity, admitting error is not a humiliation. It is the final, perfect calibration. In the workshop, you do not hide a crooked cut or a misaligned joint; you place it on the bench, run the straightedge over it, and acknowledge the deviation. To stand before the Source of all coordinates and recognize that my measurements were short, that my plumb line was crooked, and that my physics was incomplete is the ultimate act of

alignment. It is the moment the blind worker finally receives his sight and sees the house he was trying to build in the dark. It is the surrender of all post-hoc rationalizations, the final settlement of the circuit. Admitting error is the only way to clean the dial indicator and reset the machine.
Second, I will say: “Thank you.”

I will say it with the gratitude of a tradesman who has watched a structure stand under a load that should have crushed it. Thank you for preserving the timeline. Thank you for maintaining the cooperative substrate when our own hands were too small, too weak, and too distracted to hold it together. Thank you for the grace that bent the forces of history toward justice, and for the preservation of the folk who carried the memory of Your name through the dark centuries of extraction. Thank you for the gift of

a world governed by invariants, where work could be done, where geometry was reliable, and where order could be built. Thank you for the soil, the water, the wood, and the iron that made our labor possible.
And finally, I will say: “I’m sorry.”

I will say it as an apology for the limits of my sight and the friction I generated because of my blindness. In a workshop, when a worker uses a dull blade or forces a joint together, he creates friction. He heats the steel, tears the wood fibers, and makes the work harder for everyone on the crew. My skepticism was a heavy, awkward tool. I used it to keep the lines straight and to protect my mind from the Gnostic drift of the enclosure, but that tool generated heat and friction. I’m sorry for the moments I

mistook the conduit for the power, the tool for the builder, and the machine for the Designer. I’m sorry for the times my pride made me speak as if the scaffolding were the house, and for the kinetic friction I introduced into the circuit because I could not see the Hand that was bending the wires. I’m sorry for the limits of my eyes, which could only see the curvature of the spacetime manifold and not the glory that curved it.

Until that morning arrives—if it arrives—the work of the vineyard continues. The shovel is in my hands, the line is set, and the coordinates of the covenant are the only plumb line I have to steer by. The rest is in motion.
